title: Everyone has a vocation
hook: vocation means calling, and every baptized person has one

segments.voice: Yesterday, charismatic renewal: students reading Acts, a chapel at night, and Paul's gifts of grace, the charisms. Your line was come, spirit. When did those two words come in handy? Day one thousand four hundred six.

It's night in the house of God at Shiloh, and the lamp hasn't gone out yet. A boy named Samuel is asleep near the ark. A voice says his name. He jumps up and runs to the old priest, Eli: here I am, you called me. Eli says he didn't, go back to bed. It happens again. Then the text says the Lord called Samuel again the third time, and this time Eli understands. Go lie down, he tells the boy, and if it comes again, answer. It comes. And Samuel says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." A whole life starts with a name said in the dark. Today, a new stretch on callings, and today's word: vocation.
screen: `A BOY ASLEEP AT SHILOH.` → `HERE I AM, YOU CALLED ME.` → `SPEAK, LORD, FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.`

segments.voice: A vocation is a calling. It isn't first a job or a career. It's a voice, and somebody answering it. Praying for vocations can sound like praying only for priests, sisters and brothers. That's a real calling, and this stretch of days will get to it. But the Church's teaching starts wider. The Second Vatican Council said that all the faithful, whatever their state of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of love. The Catechism repeats it: the call to holiness is for everyone. It goes back to a hard sentence of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect." Not said to monks. Said on a mountain, and Matthew says the crowds heard it. So the Catholic picture runs in two layers. The first call comes to every baptized person, the same for all: to holiness, to love. Then each life answers it in a particular shape. Marriage. The single life. Religious vows. Holy orders. The coming days take those one at a time. Paul, writing from prison, puts the first layer plainly: "I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you that you walk worthy of the vocation in which you are called." He's writing to a whole church of ordinary people. Notice what that does to an ordinary Tuesday. The nurse on a night shift, the dad at the school pickup, the student cramming: none of them is waiting for a calling to arrive someday. Catholic teaching says they already have one, and they're living it, or not, right now.
screen: `A VOCATION IS A CALLING.` · `NOT ONLY PRIESTS AND SISTERS.` · `ONE CALL TO HOLINESS FOR ALL.` · `THEN A SHAPE FOR EACH LIFE.` · then, large: `WALK WORTHY OF THE VOCATION IN WHICH YOU ARE CALLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask what you're called to. Settle, and breathe. Don't ask about the next five years. Ask about this season. Who is in front of you right now, needing something only you can give? What work is in your hands this week? Let one face, or one task, come up, and stay with it. If you pray, you can borrow Samuel's words: speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth. Then listen. If you don't, simply ask the question and let it sit there, unanswered for now. The bell holds the time.
Vocation. A calling. In Catholic teaching, every baptized person's call to holiness, lived out in a particular state of life. Today's word.

Your line: called. Today, at one ordinary task, a shift, a meal, a phone call, say the word to yourself, called, and do that task as if someone had asked you by name. Day one thousand four hundred six.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of a universal call to holiness that every baptized person shares, and of particular vocations: marriage, the single life, religious life and holy orders. Parishes pray for vocations, and people discerning a calling often talk it through with a priest, sister or spiritual director.

fork.reveal: Eli understands it's the Lord calling. he sends Samuel back to listen, and Samuel answers, "speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth."

trapdoor: what you thought: a vocation is what priests and nuns have.
what it means: a calling. every baptized person is called to holiness, and each life answers in a particular shape.
what a scholar hears: the Second Vatican Council's universal call to holiness (Lumen Gentium 40), with Paul's Ephesians 4:1 behind it.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of 1 Kings (1 Samuel) 3:10, Matthew 5:48 and Ephesians 4:1: confirm.
'The Lord called Samuel again the third time' follows 1 Samuel 3:8; Samuel is described as asleep 'near the ark' per 3:3. Confirm.
Vocation from Latin vocare, to call: standard dictionary derivation; confirm.
Lumen Gentium 40 and CCC 2013 (universal call to holiness for all the faithful, of whatever state or rank): paraphrased; confirm.
'In plenty of Catholic parishes, praying for vocations has come to mean praying for priests, sisters and brothers' is a soft, unquantified claim about common usage; the editor may cut it.

The four states of life listed (marriage, the single life, religious life, holy orders) follow the coming days of this outline; confirm the Keeper is comfortable naming the single life as a vocation alongside the others.
